name: Colorado
summary_text: Colorado stands within the United States federal framework, which sets the baseline a trans visitor carries into the state: Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, the State Department no longer issues the X marker and processes new passports only as M or F, the Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and TSA screening procedures can require secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that disclose a traveller's trans status. Visa discretion over transgender athletes applying to compete in women's sports, flagged with an internal marking and treated in some cases as grounds for a permanent ban, applies at any port of entry including Denver.  State law in Colorado runs against that current. The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act expressly covers gender identity and gender expression across employment, housing and public accommodations, and the legislature expanded that coverage again in 2025. Public-accommodation coverage is the provision a visitor would rely on directly, in hotels, restaurants, shops and venues.  The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on 18 May 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law by suspending gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to enjoin the hospital into resuming puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing the same treatment for cisgender children while halting it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity.' Two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.  Care access still narrows on federal funding. Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage of hormone therapy, puberty blockers and related gender-affirming care for transgender youth from 13 October 2026, because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under 18 and under 19 through the CHP+ child programme. The state Medicaid agency says resuming coverage 'will require legislative action.' Patients already taking hormones retain coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected. A visitor needing continuing care should therefore expect the federal constraint to govern here rather than the state's protective posture.  A July 2026 national risk assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people, alongside California, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey, and counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage.  That posture faces a direct political test. Colorado voters decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender children from gendered sports not aligned with biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after elections officials certified signatures on the measures in March 2026. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and, if passed, would write restrictions on transgender minors into state law.  Incarceration risk in Colorado is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care; a court-approved 2024 consent decree in Denver District Court (Raven v. Polis) required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement, and relief has been won through court order rather than a baseline housing rule.

sources.title: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment / Division of Motor Vehicles - gender marker rules
sources.documents: Removal Feb 2019 of surgery requirement for gender change (required Jan 1, 1984 to Feb 13, 2019); current process by request via 'Change of Sex Designation' form for DL/state ID and 'Birth Certificate Correction Form' + 'Sex Designation Form' for birth certificate; minors need parent/guardian + medical/mental health professional consent; descriptors M/F/Intersex/X for birth certificates, male/female/X for IDs.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Cited as: unanimous board vote Feb 2019.

sources.title: Colorado hate-crime enforcement - 2001 law, 2009 Greeley transgender murder conviction, Club Q shooting 2022
sources.documents: Hate-crime law protections based on sexual orientation and gender identity/expression since 2001 with penalty enhancements; 2009 Greeley jury convicted man of first-degree murder as hate crime in transgender victim case - thought first applied in murder trial; Nov 2022 mass shooting at gay bar in Colorado Springs (Club Q), 305 charges, FBI investigation, red-flag law lawsuit, April 2023 emergency gun bills; reported 380% increase in sexual-orientation hate crimes since 2018.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Cited as: Greeley conviction 2009; Colorado Springs shooting Nov 2022; Dec 2022 charges; April 2023 gun laws signed; June 2023 lawsuit against Sheriff's Department.

name: Connecticut
summary_text: Connecticut is a state within the United States, and its laws stand under the national framework that governs a trans visitor's entry, identity documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Visa applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex can be treated as committing fraud and barred permanently, and since February 2025 trans athletes have been barred from entering the country to compete in women's sports, with an internal marking applied to flagged applicants.  Care access for a visitor is constrained at the federal layer. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.  Against that national backdrop, Connecticut's own law runs in the opposite direction. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, places Connecticut in a fifteen-state most-protective tier whose laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.  Connecticut also operates a shield or refuge law. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Connecticut as a state holding a shield law or executive order dating from 2022. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in Connecticut but banned in the person's home state, which makes the state directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a state with a youth-care ban.

sources.title: H.B. No. 7006 - Birth Certificate Gender Marker Law
sources.documents: Makes it easier for transgender people to change gender marker on birth certificate without surgery; establishes affidavit process and M/F/X options for birth certificates, IDs and driver's licenses
sources.detail: Passed June 2015, Senate 32-3 and House 126-18; signed by Governor Dannel Malloy; effective October 1, 2015; Department of Public Health affidavit from applicant plus physician/APRN/psychologist
